title: Japan Makes It Harder to Get Permanent Residency
paragraphs: Japan has made it more difficult for foreign residents to obtain permanent residency, as the government tightens its immigration rules.

The new guidelines, announced by Japan's Immigration Services Agency, came into effect on October 1, 2026, and will be introduced in stages. Most of the new requirements will apply to applications submitted on or after April 1, 2027. However, some of the rules on income will also apply to certain applications that were already being processed.

Under the new rules, applicants will have to show that their annual income is consistently higher than the average household income of Japanese citizens. They will also need to show that they can expect to receive pension benefits equal to those of someone who has paid into the pension system for 30 years. In addition, applicants must be able to hold everyday conversations in Japanese and show that they understand Japan's laws and social rules. Previously, the guidelines did not include specific requirements for income, pensions or language ability.

The cost of applying has also risen sharply. The application fee increased 20-fold, from 10,000 yen to 200,000 yen, on October 1. Before the fee increase, hundreds of people lined up at an immigration office in central Tokyo to submit their applications, with some waiting for up to five hours.

The changes are part of a push by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi to tighten immigration controls. Takaichi has said that she wants "orderly coexistence" with foreign residents. Immigration has become an important political issue in Japan, and false claims on social media, such as claims that foreigners receive a large share of welfare payments, have spread widely.

However, many experts and business leaders argue that Japan needs more foreign workers, because of its low birth rate, aging population and labor shortages. Permanent residency offers foreign residents long-term stability and the freedom to work in any job. Without it, people often find it difficult to get a mortgage. The new rules are not expected to force anyone to leave the country immediately, but they may discourage some people from applying.
